questions: Why do the rectangle estimates get closer to 8/3 as the slices get thinner?
What would a left-endpoint estimate do differently on this increasing curve?
segments.say: Riemann sums: slicing area under a curve. An integral begins life as a sum - slice the interval under y = x^2 from 0 to 2, stand a rectangle on each slice, and add. Four rectangles give 3.75, eight give 3.1875, and the exact area 8/3 is what those sums are converging to. Keep that picture in mind all lesson: every integral is a limit of sums first.

questions: Where does the graph of y = x cross the axis, and why does that point matter?
What is the difference between the integral from -1 to 2 and the total area from -1 to 2?
segments.say: Signed area: below the axis counts negative. The line y = x from -1 to 2 makes two triangles: +2 above the axis and -0.5 below it, so the integral is 3/2, the net. Say it plainly: an integral reports signed area, and if a question wants total area you split at the crossing and add magnitudes yourself.

questions: How do you decide which part of the integrand should become u?
What three things must change when you substitute - and what goes wrong if one is left in x?
segments.say: U-substitution: the chain rule in reverse. In the integral of 2x e^(x^2) from 0 to 1, the 2x outside is precisely the derivative of the x^2 inside. Set u = x^2 and du = 2x dx, rewrite the whole line - integrand, differential and limits - and the integral collapses to the integral of e^u, which is e - 1. Check your student notes for the bookkeeping checklist before the worksheet.

questions: Why is the radius of each disc x^2 and not x?
Where have you seen the slice-add-and-take-the-limit pattern earlier in this lesson?
segments.say: Volumes of revolution: stacking discs. Rotate y = x^2 about the x-axis from 0 to 1 and the curve sweeps out a solid. Slice it across the axis: every slice is nearly a disc of radius x^2 and thickness dx, volume pi (x^2)^2 dx. Stack the discs - a Riemann sum again - and the volume is pi times the integral of x^4 from 0 to 1, which is pi/5. Now open the worksheet and try the disc question in pairs.
segments.watchFor: A definite integral still needs the +C in the answer. Watch for it on the worksheet volume question too: students who add +C to a volume have carried the indefinite habit into a definite answer - a volume is one number.

questions: State, in one sentence, exactly when +C must be written.
In the exit ticket, which question is most likely to tempt you into adding +C - and how will you catch it?
segments.say: The +C trap: only for indefinite integrals. An indefinite integral names a family, so it earns its +C. A definite integral evaluates at two limits, and the constant cancels in the subtraction - from 1 to 2 the answer is simply 7/3. Compare the trap section of your student notes one last time. Now the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - covering signed area, substitution and the disc volume.
segments.watchFor: A definite integral still needs the +C in the answer. Listen and look for it as the exit ticket comes in: any definite answer wearing a +C shows the habit, not the understanding - send them back to (8/3 + C) - (1/3 + C) = 7/3.
